title: Zero-Data Self-Play: Absolute Zero, R-Zero, Agent0

questions.question: Absolute Zero, R-Zero and Agent0 are described as 'zero-data' methods. What exactly do they remove from the RLVR recipe?
options: All external grounding: the model grades its own answers by introspection alone
Human-written tasks and labels; an executor or a consistency check still supplies the ground truth
The reinforcement-learning stage; the policy is trained by supervised fine-tuning on its own outputs
The base model's pretraining data; the policy starts from randomly initialized weights
questions.explanation: Zero data means zero external tasks and labels, not zero grounding. AZR keeps a Python executor and R-Zero/Agent0 keep majority vote over the solver's samples, which is why the verifier's strength sets the loop's ceiling.

questions.question: In AZR's abduction mode the solver is given a program and an output and must produce an input. How does the executor decide whether the solver's input is correct?
options: It compares the solver's input to the original input the proposer used, character by character
It asks the proposer role to confirm that the solver's input is the one it originally had in mind
It runs the solver's input through a majority vote over ten other sampled candidate inputs
It runs the program on the solver's proposed input and checks that the result equals the given output
questions.explanation: Programs need not be injective, so any input that maps to the given output is correct. The executor re-runs the program rather than comparing to the proposer's original input.

questions.question: R-Zero rewards the Challenger with 1 - 2|p - 1/2|, where p is the Solver's empirical agreement rate. Why does this favour tasks around p = 0.5 rather than the hardest tasks the Solver can still occasionally solve?
options: Mixed success/failure groups carry the most gradient under group-normalized RL; all-pass and all-fail groups give zero advantage
Tasks at p = 0.5 are the cheapest to verify because half of the attempts can be skipped once the majority answer is known
The reward is a proxy for difficulty: harder tasks always have lower p, so rewarding 0.5 is a compromise with throughput
Human-written benchmarks have about a 50% average solve rate, so matching that rate keeps the curriculum on-distribution
questions.explanation: GRPO normalizes rewards within a group, so a group where every attempt agrees produces zero advantages. The chance of a mixed group and the spread of rewards inside it both peak at p = 0.5, which is also where the outcome entropy is one bit.

questions.question: R-Zero labels each self-generated question with the majority vote of the Solver's ten answers and keeps questions with 3 to 7 agreeing samples. What did the paper measure about these pseudo-labels as training progressed?
options: Their accuracy against GPT-4o ground truth stayed above 95% because the consistency band removes ambiguous questions
Their accuracy rose from 63% to 79% as the Solver improved, so later iterations needed less filtering than early ones
Their accuracy against GPT-4o ground truth fell from 79% at step 15 to 69% at step 30 and 63% by the third iteration
Their accuracy could not be measured because the generated questions had no reference answers in any external source
questions.explanation: Section 4.4 of R-Zero reports 79.0% -> 69.0% -> 63.0%. The curriculum walks toward harder questions, which is exactly where majority vote is least reliable.

questions.question: Agent0 adds a sandboxed Python interpreter to the executor agent and a tool-use term to the curriculum agent's reward. Which ceiling of the self-play loop does this move?
options: The verifier's accuracy ceiling: the interpreter replaces majority vote with real execution on every task
The task-space ceiling: with a tool the solver sometimes solves tasks beyond its unaided ability, so the frontier moves higher
The compute ceiling: tool calls are cheaper than extra samples, so more tasks fit in the same training budget
The context-length ceiling: the interpreter stores intermediate results outside the model's window
questions.explanation: A proposer can only pose tasks the base model can imagine and a solver can only learn tasks it sometimes solves. Tools let the executor solve harder tasks, which pulls the curriculum agent's frontier upward; Agent0 still uses majority-vote pseudo-labels for the reward.

questions.question: In code/main.py, raising --verifier-fp from 0 to 0.25 drops final skill from 8.63 to 2.08 under the learnability reward. Which chain of effects explains the collapse?
options: False positives shrink the proposer's reward, so it retreats to trivial tasks where the solver learns nothing new
False positives add noise to the executor's timing, so fewer tasks are validated per round and learning slows down
False positives inflate the observed solve rate: the proposer poses harder tasks while the solver trains on wrong solutions
False positives are ignored by the proposer but counted twice by the solver, which then overfits to the easy tasks
questions.explanation: Both roles only see what the verifier accepted. The inflated p-hat tells the proposer the frontier is higher than it is, and every accepted-but-wrong solution pulls the solver's skill down; the run shows observed 34.4% vs true 13.5% solve rate at the end.
